teaching_point: Pyogenic granuloma, new lesion on the finger.

teaching_point: The same PG 2 weeks later. Rapid growth over days to weeks after minor trauma is typical.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — 2 weeks later (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/pyogenic-granuloma

teaching_point: The same PG at 4 weeks: pedunculated, friable. Bleeding on contact is the usual reason people present.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — 4 weeks after first photograph (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/pyogenic-granuloma

teaching_point: Dermoscopy: red clods separated by white lines (collarette). Vessels are not diagnostic, and amelanotic melanoma can look similar.
dermnet_caption: Red clods separated by white lines in pyogenic granuloma
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Red clods separated by white lines in pyogenic granuloma (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/pyogenic-granuloma

teaching_point: Crusted, bleeding PG on a finger. Cryotherapy and silver nitrate give no specimen and recur more.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Pyogenic granuloma (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/pyogenic-granuloma

teaching_point: Excision wound immediately after removal of a facial skin cancer. Warn the patient the wound is longer than the lesion (ellipse about 3:1).
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Excision wound (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/excision-of-skin-lesions

teaching_point: The same wound sutured. Face sutures usually come out at about 5–7 days; neck, trunk and limbs later (local protocol).
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Sutured wound (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/excision-of-skin-lesions

teaching_point: The healed scar. Scars mature over 12–18 months; massage and sun protection help.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Healed wound (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/excision-of-skin-lesions

teaching_point: Ellipse marked along relaxed skin tension lines, which gives a finer scar.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Excision selecting relaxed tension lines (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/skin-tension-lines

teaching_point: Surgical wound dehiscence on the neck. Causes are tension, infection, haematoma or early activity.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Surgical wound dehiscence (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/risks-and-complications-of-skin-surgery

teaching_point: Dehisced wound on a limb with infection and haematoma risk. Anticoagulated patients need good aftercare and a clear plan for bleeding.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Surgical wound dehiscence (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/risks-and-complications-of-skin-surgery

teaching_point: Hypertrophic scar: raised but confined to the wound margins, and it often improves over months.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Hypertrophic scar (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/risks-and-complications-of-skin-surgery

teaching_point: Atrophic (stretched) scar. This is common on the back and shoulders, where tension is high.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Atrophic scar (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/risks-and-complications-of-skin-surgery

teaching_point: Large post-surgical presternal keloid: it extends beyond the wound. High-risk sites are the chest, shoulders, earlobes and upper back. Avoid elective surgery there in keloid-prone patients.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — A large post-surgical presternal keloid (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/images/keloid-and-hypertrophic-scar-images

teaching_point: Earlobe keloid after piercing. Ask about personal or family keloids at consent.
dermnet_caption: A keloid on the earlobe after piercing
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — A keloid on the earlobe after piercing (© Dr Richard Ashton) — https://dermnetnz.org/images/keloid-and-hypertrophic-scar-images

teaching_point: Cryotherapy blister 48 hours after treatment. This is an expected reaction: keep it clean and leave the roof intact.
dermnet_caption: A cryotherapy blister 48 hrs after treatment
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — A cryotherapy blister 48 hrs after treatment (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cryotherapy

teaching_point: Haemorrhagic blisters 3 days after cryotherapy on the hands. More likely with anticoagulants or antiplatelets. It is not a reason to stop them.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Haemorrhagic blisters 3 days after treatment (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cryotherapy

teaching_point: Eyelid oedema 24 hours after cryotherapy near the nose. Warn about this for facial treatment; it settles in days.
dermnet_caption: Eyelid oedema 24 hrs after cryotherapy to the lesion adjacent to the nose
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Eyelid oedema 24 hrs after cryotherapy to the lesion adjacent to the nose (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cryotherapy

teaching_point: Recurrent BCC after cryotherapy. Destructive treatment without histology risks missing or under-treating cancer.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Recurrent BCC post-cryotherapy (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/cryotherapy

teaching_point: Positive latex skin prick test (type I allergy, a wheal). Confirms immediate-type latex allergy, so the patient needs a latex-free environment.
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — A positive latex prick test (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/latex-allergy

teaching_point: Immediate type I reaction (facial urticaria/angioedema) after contact with a rubber balloon. Severe reactions can be anaphylaxis: adrenaline 500 micrograms IM (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL) in adults, per the course and UK Resuscitation Council.
dermnet_caption: An immediate type 1 reaction after exposure to a rubber balloon; the cheeks and lids have swollen in the last 10 minutes
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — An immediate type 1 reaction after exposure to a rubber balloon; the cheeks and lids have swollen in the last 10 minutes (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/latex-allergy

teaching_point: Recurrent BCC, a classic Mohs indication (BAD 2021: recurrent BCC with another high-risk factor, or high-risk facial sites).
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Recurrent basal cell carcinoma (© DermNet) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/mohs-micrographic-surgery

teaching_point: Skin flap reconstruction 12 months after a large BCC excision on the nose. The final cosmetic result takes up to a year.
dermnet_caption: Skin flap reconstruction 12 months after a large BCC excision
licence_note: DermNet image licence: https://dermnetnz.org/image-licence (watermarked low-res; personal/educational use with attribution)
attribution: Image: DermNet — Skin flap reconstruction 12 months after a large BCC excision (© Te Whatu Ora) — https://dermnetnz.org/topics/flaps

teaching_point: Established full-thickness skin graft on the nose after skin cancer removal. Colour and contour mismatch is common early on.
dermnet_caption: The established full thickness skin graft after skin cancer removal on the nose
